approved: Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment (2014 Measures No. 4) Bill 2014

Outlined Labor's support for abolishing the mature age tax offset and updating deductible gift recipients, but opposition to R&D and seafarer tax offset changes, citing a $620 million cut to the R&D tax concession and a $115 million cut to the CSIRO, while contrasting this with a Paid Parental Leave scheme that could pay up to $50,000 per birth.

Praised the government for implementing Labor's multinational tax avoidance measures in the No. 4 bill, which built on a plan Labor said would have stopped $5 billion moving offshore, credited former Assistant Treasurer David Bradbury, now advising the OECD on tax reform, and condemned the government for instead reopening $1.1 billion in other tax loopholes for multinationals.

Responded to the member for McMahon's tax bill remarks with personal banter, conceding he was unlikely to become the next Assistant Treasurer but joking he was closer to higher office than his opponent.

Criticised the government's priorities, noting it gave superannuation tax cuts to the 20,000 wealthiest people in the system while reopening $1.1 billion in multinational tax loopholes, contrasted with Labor's closure of similar loopholes worth $5.3 billion while in government, and said the bill's thin capitalisation changes were welcome but only a fraction of what Labor had planned.

Opposed abolishing the seafarer tax offset, part of Labor's Stronger Shipping reforms, noting Australia's shipping fleet had fallen from 55 to 21 ships over a decade with only four now on international routes, and said the offset cost just $8 million over the forward estimates, a small price to protect the industry.

Criticised the government for opposing Labor's 2012 multinational profit-shifting reforms worth $1.1 billion while in opposition, noted Labor's phase-out of the mature age worker tax offset for those born before 1 July 1957 was expected to raise $255 million, and opposed abolishing the seafarer tax offset less than two years after it began in July 2012.

Supported the Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment bills, highlighting integrity measures expected to raise about $755 million over four years, and championed the government's new one-page personalised tax receipt showing taxpayers where their money is spent, recalling that Australia's net government debt was last fully repaid on 'debt-free day' in April 2006.

Defended the Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment bills as part of the government's plan to pay off the $123 billion in deficits inherited from Labor, noting the government inherited a backlog of 96 announced but unlegislated tax measures, and highlighted that the bill raises the thin-capitalisation de minimis threshold from $250,000 to $2 million to cut compliance costs for small business.
Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment (2014 Measures No. 4) Act 2014
